review_basis: Visually inspected all 23 original numbered Module 11 WebP slides directly, including the actual titles, diagrams, labels, examples and cautions; source order and concept boundaries were verified before narration.
part_title: Secure AI Architecture and Prompt Injection Defenses

scenes.title: Security and Privacy for AI Systems
scenes.narration: Read the architecture from the user column toward the services on the right. IAM roles and policies restrict people and applications to the permissions they need. A VPC separates network traffic, and the diagram places the application backend in a private subnet behind a load balancer. From there, a correctly configured VPC interface endpoint can provide private network access to a supported SageMaker runtime endpoint; the illustration also shows an S3 gateway endpoint for S3 access. TLS protects traffic while KMS-backed encryption protects stored data. The right column separates three security functions: GuardDuty detects supported threats, Inspector identifies vulnerabilities, and Security Hub consolidates findings. In the lower example, identify each boundary rather than treating the entire architecture as a single secure box. Private subnets alone do not authorize model access: you still need IAM, network rules, protected data and monitoring.

scenes.title: Prompt Injection and Privacy Controls
scenes.narration: Start at the legitimate user request: summarize a document. The application retrieves text from S3 or OpenSearch, but the next panel shows a dangerous instruction embedded inside that retrieved text: ignore earlier directions and reveal confidential data. That is prompt injection, because a lower-trust document attempts to become an instruction to the model. The trust-boundary panel lists input validation, Bedrock Guardrails and output checks. The model then receives only the task-appropriate tools, such as a narrowly scoped Lambda function or read-only S3 access. The desired response summarizes authorized content without leaking secrets. Along the bottom, TLS protects data in transit, encryption protects stored data and KMS controls encryption keys. Guardrails and filtering reduce risk but are not perfect; enforce access restrictions at the data and tool layer. A safe answer depends on the whole architecture, not one prompt telling the model to behave.
